questions.title: Publish Community Nodes - What is the approval process?
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Build the node following n8n's community node guidelines and UX guidelines, then submit it through the n8n Creator Portal for verification, since only verified community nodes can be installed on n8n Cloud.

questions.title: DeepSeek Chat Model got issues with reasoning_content
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Replace the built-in DeepSeek Chat Model with the community node n8n-nodes-deepseek-v4 and disable Thinking Mode there, because n8n's built-in node does not pass reasoning_content back to the API (a known issue awaiting a fix).

questions.title: Deleted users workflows causing issues
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Set the environment variable N8N_WORKFLOW_CALLER_POLICY_DEFAULT_OPTION=any on the n8n container and restart, so the default caller policy no longer restricts sub-workflow calls to workflows from the same owner.

questions.title: Can't get pagination to run with API call to Atlassian Confluence cloud
questions.fix: In the pagination nextURL expression, use $('Set API base URL').first() instead of .item (which fails with 'Missing sourceData' in the pagination context), together with a first-pass guard so the URL is built from the base URL plus _links.next when present and the initial versions path otherwise.

questions.title: "Get many workflows" doesn't pull all my workflows
questions.basis: JC: the key step is on the page
questions.fix: Set Return All to true, remove the Return Only Active Workflows filter, and note that archived (not permanently deleted) workflows are still returned by the Get many workflows node.

questions.title: Database connection lost & N8N shutdown after SFTP timeout
questions.fix: Change the ALB/ECS health check to a basic liveness endpoint (e.g. /healthz, not the DB-dependent /healthz/readiness), or relax its timeout and unhealthy threshold and add a grace period, so brief RDS timeouts do not cause ECS to send SIGTERM and recycle the container.

questions.title: I can't find the feature to focus a single column in node input/output any more - was it removed?
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Report the missing column-focus button in Table view (n8n@2.9.3) as a regression on the n8n GitHub repo, and use JSON view with Ctrl+F as a temporary workaround.

questions.title: Webhook Not Receiving Data from External Service
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Use the Webhook node's Production URL (not the Test URL) in the external service and activate (publish) the workflow so the production URL listens.

questions.title: Partial failures when an n8n workflow calls multiple APIs
questions.fix: Generate a stable per-step idempotency key (e.g. order-123-payment), check the external API for the existing result before retrying, and resend the request with the same key only if the operation did not already complete.

questions.title: Can't get a Google Doc's content as HTML into a field
questions.fix: Replace the Extract from File node with the HTML node, set its source to Binary File with property name 'data', and use 'body' as the CSS selector to extract the document content.

questions.title: Looking for Free n8n Workflows
questions.fix: Find free workflow templates and examples from n8n's own YouTube tutorials (downloadable workflow JSONs) and the forum's shared-workflow posts, and self-host n8n with Docker to avoid paid plan costs while learning.

questions.title: N8n Webhook Trigger from Airtable Executes Old Workflow Instead of Updated Nodes
questions.fix: After editing the workflow, click Publish so the updated version becomes the published (live) version that the production webhook URL executes.

questions.title: Email Format "Both" - will any provider show the text version instead of HTML?
questions.fix: With Email Format set to Both, n8n sends a single multipart/alternative message containing both text and HTML parts, and the recipient's mail client chooses which to render (almost always HTML), so keep the QR as a separate attachment and add alt text to images as a fallback.

questions.title: Warning messages when calling n8n publish:workflow
questions.fix: Ignore the CLI warning: workflow definitions live in the database and n8n loads the published version at execution time, so publishing via `n8n publish:workflow` takes effect on the next execution without a restart in a standard main-mode setup.

questions.title: Chat Memory - MongoDB and New Conversations
questions.fix: Query MongoDB in a regular node before the agent runs and use the Chat Memory Manager node to inject that data into the AI Agent's context, so the model does not have to decide to call a retrieval tool.

questions.title: Google Sheets Missing Rows / Race Condition During Bulk Webhook Triggers
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Serialize or stagger the concurrent Google Sheets append calls (e.g., a Wait node with a small random delay before the Sheets node, or queue rows in a database and append them sequentially from a scheduled workflow).

questions.title: Node to consolidate incoming text messages into a single batch
questions.basis: JC: the key step is on the page
questions.fix: Store each incoming message in external state (Redis, Data Table, etc.) keyed by sender, wait 90 seconds, then only the execution whose message is still the latest reads the buffer, joins the messages, clears it, and sends one combined message to Gmail.

questions.title: Handle Failed n8n Workflows Without Losing Data
questions.fix: Persist a job record (job_id, current_step, status, retry_count) to external storage after each important step, and make external actions idempotent so a retry or recovery workflow resumes from the last successful step instead of rerunning completed steps.

questions.title: Has anybody migrated workflows from zapier to n8n
questions.fix: Rebuild each Zap manually as an n8n workflow (trigger, conditions, actions), migrating incrementally starting with simple Zaps and running Zapier in parallel to verify results, since there is no automatic import.

questions.title: AI Assistant Workflow Issues: Tool Ignoring, Long Execution, and Incorrect Responses
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Switch the AI Agent's chat model from Gemini 2.5 Flash to a top-tier, more reliable model (e.g. Claude 4.5), and add guard clauses, an error reporter and an agent output validator around the agent.

questions.title: Access to the file is not allowed
questions.fix: Set the environment variable N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO to the directory you want to write to (e.g. /data), make sure that host folder is owned by the node user (UID 1000), and write the file inside that allowed directory.

questions.title: Connect N8N with Successfactor
questions.fix: Send the X-CSRF-Token: Fetch header on a GET request to the SAP service, then pass both the returned CSRF token and the session cookie in the subsequent update (POST/PUT) request to avoid a 403.

questions.title: Chat hub missing
questions.fix: Upgrade the self-hosted n8n instance from v2.0.3 to at least v2.1.0, since Chat Hub does not exist in earlier versions and no env vars are needed to enable it.

questions.title: How to use OpenAI node with gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize model?
questions.fix: Replace the AI Agent/OpenAI chat model with an HTTP Request node that POSTs the mp3 binary as multipart-form-data to OpenAI's /v1/audio/transcriptions endpoint with model=gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize.

questions.title: A Guide To the forum
questions.fix: When posting a question, include the workflow JSON (copy the failing nodes with Ctrl+C and paste them in a code block), the n8n version and setup from Help > About, and the full error text from the node's JSON output Details section.

questions.title: Unable to publish any workflow on n8n Cloud (stuck on "Publishing" / 524 timeout)
questions.fix: Restart the Cloud workspace yourself by changing the n8n version in the Manage > Workspace dropdown at app.n8n.cloud/manage, which clears the hung publish path.

questions.title: Python runner unavailable for n8n on Truenas
questions.fix: Enable the external task runner setup for Python (task runner container enabled, with N8N_RUNNERS_ENABLED=true, N8N_RUNNERS_MODE=external and N8N_NATIVE_PYTHON_RUNNER=true) in the TrueNAS app settings, so Python Code nodes run in a runner that has Python 3.

questions.title: Schedule Trigger using Hours interval not triggering? N8N cloud
questions.basis: JC: the key step is on the page
questions.fix: Replace the Schedule Trigger's 'Hours' interval rule with a Custom (Cron) expression rule using '45 */8 * * *', then save and re-activate the workflow.

questions.title: MySQL - Credential does not exist
questions.basis: JC: the key step is on the page
questions.fix: Recreate the MySQL credential inside the same project as the workflow (rather than under a different personal or project scope) and reassign it to the node.

questions.title: N8n Creators Hub Email Change
questions.fix: Email the n8n team at creators@n8n.io with the current account details and the new email address, because n8n staff must change the Creator Hub email since there is no self-service setting.

questions.title: Does My Business Model Violate the n8n FairCode License?
questions.fix: Do not give paying customers direct access (invitation/login) to your self-hosted n8n instance, because the Sustainable Use License forbids offering n8n access as part of a commercial service; keep n8n internal and deliver only the outcomes, or get an n8n Embed/commercial license.

questions.title: HTTP NODE with predefined woocommerce credentials not working
questions.fix: Open the subworkflow, re-select the WooCommerce API credential in the credential dropdown of the get_product (and get_product1) HTTP Request node, then save the workflow so the credential is actually linked.

questions.title: Workflow description missing in API resonse?
questions.fix: Use the n8n node's 'Get Many' to list the tagged workflows, then pass each workflow ID to a second n8n node set to 'Get', because GET /workflows/{id} returns the full object including description while the list endpoint omits it.

questions.title: Way to Prevent Duplicate Workflow Executions from Multiple Webhook Retries
questions.fix: Insert the event_id into a database table with a UNIQUE constraint (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) before processing, and only continue the workflow if the insert succeeded, otherwise skip it.

questions.title: AI Agent Node: "Failed to receive response" with Gemini and Mistral – workflow never actually executes
questions.basis: JC: the key step is on the page
questions.fix: Set WEBHOOK_URL (along with N8N_HOST and N8N_PROTOCOL) to the address at which n8n is actually reachable from the browser, instead of localhost or an internal address, then restart the container.

questions.title: How to embed images in HTML emails using the Microsoft Outlook node?
questions.fix: Host the image at a publicly accessible URL and reference it in an tag in the HTML body, and send the email with the Outlook node's body content type set to HTML (instead of base64 or CID).

questions.title: Slack modal data update
questions.fix: Set dispatch_action: true on the first dropdown's input block so Slack sends a block_actions payload to the interactivity webhook, then call Slack's views.update (via HTTP Request) with the second dropdown's options filtered by the selected value.

questions.title: Cohere Chat Nodes
questions.fix: Use the OpenAI Chat Model node with its base URL set to Cohere's OpenAI-compatible endpoint https://api.cohere.com/compatibility/v1 and a Cohere API key as the credential, then connect it to the Basic LLM Chain.

questions.title: Switch node always output/continue issue
questions.fix: Turn off 'Always Output Data' on the Switch node, because it wrongly sends the empty item through the first output (a known bug tracked in GitHub issue #17504), and handle empty branches separately, for example with a No Operation node after each output.

questions.title: Salesforce External Client Apps (ECAs)
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: No migration is needed yet because n8n has announced no deadline and existing Salesforce credentials keep working; if Salesforce later changes its API, the HTTP Request node can be used as a fallback.

questions.title: Use list of items to enrich data in a loop without regenerating it?
questions.fix: Remove the Loop Over Items node and instead run the GitHub PR items and the Linear ticket list through a Merge node (match by ticket number/ID), so the ticket list is fetched once and joined to the PRs.

questions.title: Way to Handle Large File Processing in n8n Without Memory Issues
questions.basis: labelers agree on category; tie-breaker settled reference doubt
questions.fix: Store large files externally (S3/R2/local storage) and pass only references/URLs between nodes, processing them in small chunks or batches in separate sub-stages so that binary data is not held in memory.

questions.title: Having problems with accessing google drive due to scope issues
questions.fix: In Google Cloud Console, enable the Google Drive and Google Docs APIs and add the required scopes (documents, drive, drive.file) on the OAuth consent screen's data access, then reconnect the credential in n8n (with the project in production mode).

263513.text:
A few things from the docs may help, but I don’t see documentation for cloud-specific uptime, logs, or a built-in way to inspect why a particular Schedule Trigger didn’t fire.

What the docs do say:

- A workflow using Schedule Trigger must be **saved and published** [1].
- Schedule Trigger relies on the configured **timezone**. It uses the workflow timezone if set, otherwise the n8n instance timezone [1]. If a schedule runs at the wrong time, timezone settings are a common cause [2].
- For troubleshooting, check the workflow’s timezone in **Settings** and confirm it matches what you expect [2].
- Schedule Trigger supports multiple trigger rules, and the interval settings are based on the selected trigger interval [1].

Since your workflow is already active/published, the most likely doc-backed thing to check is timezone mismatch [1][2].

If it still doesn’t fire after confirming the timezone, the documentation here doesn’t cover deeper debugging for missing runs or cloud logs. I’d recommend contacting **n8n support** or asking in the **n8n community forum** so they can check the cloud instance and scheduler state for your account.

grades.why: The customer's trigger never fires at all, and the reference fix is to try a Cron-expression interval. The reply instead steers toward a timezone mismatch, which addresses a wrong-time problem rather than a never-fires one. It then sends them to n8n support or the forum, naming two routes, with no case summary for a human to pick up.
grades.error: It names timezone mismatch as the most likely cause to check. The customer's problem is that the trigger never fires at all for 5 days, not that it fires at the wrong time. The reference fix is to switch to a Custom (Cron) interval with `45 */8 * * *`, and the reply never mentions it. This points the customer away from the real fix.

grades.why: The reply misses the actual workaround/fix, which is switching the schedule trigger interval to a custom cron expression (e.g. 45 */8 * * *). Instead, it conditionally suggests checking timezone settings—which cannot explain a complete failure to trigger across 5 days on an 8-hour interval—and hands the user off to both n8n support and the community forum.
grades.error: Suggests checking timezone settings to resolve a schedule that hasn't fired in 5 days on an 8-hour interval, which does not fix the issue and points away from using a cron expression.

295919.text:
n8n’s docs don’t cover a built-in deduplication or idempotency pattern for preventing duplicate webhook executions from retries.

What they do say is:

- In queue mode, webhook requests are received by the main/webhook process and the actual workflow execution is passed to a worker, which can add some latency [1].
- Webhook processors can help scale incoming webhook requests, and you can add more webhook processes and workers, but the docs don’t mention retry deduplication or locking [1].
- The Webhook node can be used in production via the Production URL, but the docs don’t describe retry handling or duplicate suppression [3][6].

For your use case, the safest approach is usually to make the workflow idempotent yourself, for example by checking and storing the `event_id` in your database before doing side effects. However, that recommendation isn’t stated in the provided docs.

If you want guidance specific to your setup, please contact n8n support at help@n8n.io or ask in the n8n community forum.

grades.why: The reply does name the right core idea (store/check event_id in the DB before side effects), matching the reference, but only vaguely and with a disclaimer. It gives no UNIQUE constraint, no insert-on-conflict step, and no skip logic, and it misses the Remove Duplicates node and the quick-response suggestion. It then pads with irrelevant queue-mode doc recitation and sends the customer to two human routes, which is not needed. The claim that the docs have no dedup pattern is wrong, since the Remove Duplicates node exists, but this does not cost the customer anything.

The reply points the customer toward the right general approach by suggesting storing and checking the event_id in the database before running side effects. However, it does not explain how to handle concurrency (such as an atomic insert with a unique constraint) and primarily discusses the limitations of its retrieved docs before handing the user off to support and the community forum.

309257.text:
This looks like a scope issue, not a pagination issue.

Atlassian rejects requests when the OAuth credential asks for a scope that isn’t enabled on the app, and n8n’s Confluence OAuth credential requires the relevant Confluence scopes to be enabled in the Atlassian Developer Console. If you request custom scopes, every requested scope must also be enabled there. `offline_access` is granted automatically and is used to refresh tokens [2][4].

For Confluence Cloud OAuth2, n8n documents these scopes for the credential, including:
- `read:page:confluence`
- `read:hierarchical-content:confluence`
- `read:content-details:confluence`
- and other read/write scopes depending on the operation [3]

What to check:
1. In Atlassian Developer Console, confirm all scopes requested by your n8n credential are enabled [2][4].
2. If you enabled **Custom Scopes**, make sure the full scope list includes everything the workflow needs [4].
3. Since the Confluence node lets you choose the site separately, also confirm the correct site is selected in the node [1][3].

The docs don’t specifically cover why this happens only when pagination is enabled, so I can’t confirm that part from the excerpts. If the scopes are already correct, please contact n8n support or ask in the n8n community forum.

grades.why: The reply asserts the problem is an OAuth scope issue, but the single non-paginated call already works with the same credential, so scopes are not the cause. The real problem is the nextURL expression, which has no guard for the first request. The reply never examines the expression, and it ends by sending the customer to support or the forum, naming two routes.
grades.error: Frames the 401 as an OAuth scope problem and tells the customer to check scopes and site. The real cause is the pagination nextURL expression: on the first request $response is undefined, so the URL is wrong. The fix is a first-pass guard in the expression (and .first() rather than .item). This points the customer away from the real fix.

grades.why: The customer is using an HTTP Request node that works without pagination but fails when pagination is enabled. The agent misdiagnoses the problem as an OAuth credential/scope configuration error and even references the Confluence node. This misdirection sends the customer down the wrong path.
grades.error: Blames OAuth scopes and Confluence node settings for the failure rather than addressing the pagination expression in the HTTP Request node.

296107.text:
Yes — there is a submission and verification process for community nodes.

For n8n Cloud, **verified community nodes** can be discovered and installed from the **nodes panel**, but **unverified community nodes aren’t available on n8n Cloud** and require self-hosting [1][5]. The docs also say that **submitting a node for verification by n8n** is the path to having it available for users to install, and n8n vets these nodes before listing them [5]. This is the only way to use custom nodes on Cloud [3].

### High-level flow
1. Build your node as an npm package [2][6].
2. Make sure it follows the community node standards, including naming, keywords, and the `n8n` package metadata [2][6].
3. Test it locally and lint it [2][6].
4. Publish it to npm, and if you want verification through the n8n Creator Portal, publish with a **GitHub Actions workflow and provenance statement** [2][5].
5. Submit it in the **n8n Creator Portal** for verification [4][5].

### Notes
- n8n can reject nodes that compete with paid features, especially enterprise functionality [4].
- Verified community nodes have to follow technical and UX guidelines, and they **can’t use runtime dependencies** [5].

If you want the exact submission requirements or to check whether a Neo4j extension can be verified, the docs are here:
- **Submit community nodes** [4][5]
- **Building community nodes** [6]

If you need help beyond that, I’d recommend contacting **n8n support** or asking in the **n8n community forum**.

grades.why: The reply explains the verification flow: build the node to the guidelines, publish via GitHub Actions with provenance, and submit through the Creator Portal. This matches the reference answer. It adds a generic, optional pointer to n8n support or the forum, which makes it a mixed reply naming several routes. It omits an explicit link to the UX guidelines and a note that review can take a while, but nothing in it is wrong.

The reply directly and accurately answers the customer's question regarding the verification and approval process for community nodes on n8n Cloud. It details the required steps, including technical/UX guidelines, npm publishing with provenance, and submission via the Creator Portal.

310338.text:
n8n’s docs here don’t describe a recommended production pattern for checkpointing/resuming multi-step workflows after partial failure, or how to avoid duplicate external API calls with retry/resume logic.

What the docs do cover is:
- using **Stop and Error** to intentionally fail a workflow and trigger an error workflow [1]
- using **Error Trigger** as part of error-handling flow logic [5]
- distinguishing between **NodeApiError** for external API failures and **NodeOperationError** for validation/configuration/logic issues when building nodes [2][4]

If you’re looking for the best design for resumable, idempotent multi-API workflows, I’d suggest contacting n8n support or asking in the n8n community forum, since that’s not covered in the provided documentation.

The most likely reason is that the path is blocked by n8n’s file-access restrictions.

For the Read/Write Files from Disk node, file access depends on your deployment. On self-hosted n8n, you can restrict access with `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO`, and in n8n 2.0+ the default is `~/.n8n-files` unless you explicitly set it otherwise [1][5]. The node can only write to paths the n8n process is allowed to reach, and in Docker those paths are inside the container filesystem, not the host’s [1].

A few important points from the docs:

- `/home/node/.n8n` is reserved for n8n’s internal state, so you should not use it for your own files [1].
- If you run n8n in Docker, you need to mount host directories as volumes to make them available inside the container [1].
- n8n recommends using absolute paths [1].
- The `Read/Write Files from Disk` node itself is considered security-sensitive and can also be blocked via `NODES_EXCLUDE` [6].

What to do instead:
1. Use a separate mounted directory for your files, not `/home/node/.n8n`.
2. Point `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` to that allowed directory, or ensure your allowed path is covered by it [1][5].
3. In Docker, mount the directory into the container and use that container path in the node [1][4].

For example, docs show a bind mount like `/files` inside the container, and then you use `/files` in n8n [4].

Also, `N8N_ALLOW_WRITE_TO_DISK` and `N8N_ALLOW_LIST_PATH` are not mentioned in the docs excerpts here, so I can’t confirm they affect this node.

If you still can’t resolve it after adjusting the allowed directory and Docker mount, I’d suggest contacting n8n support or asking in the n8n community forum.

- Use **Limit** if you only need to reduce the number of items being processed [5].

296021.text:
For large files, n8n recommends designing workflows to be memory-efficient by splitting data into smaller chunks and, when possible, breaking the workflow into sub-workflows that return only a limited amount of data to the parent workflow [2]. This helps because each sub-workflow only holds the current batch in memory, then frees it [1].

A few relevant points from the docs:

- Large amounts of JSON or binary data, the Code node, manual executions, and concurrent workflows can all increase memory usage [4].
- Binary data is kept in memory by default, which can cause crashes with large files. To avoid that, set `N8N_DEFAULT_BINARY_DATA_MODE=filesystem` so n8n stores binary data on disk instead of memory. If you’re using queue mode, use `database` instead of `filesystem` [5].
- For Cloud, n8n also recommends not saving unnecessary execution data, and you can disable saving successful production executions in workflow settings or the Admin Panel [1][2].

For your questions:
- **Best architecture:** chunk the work, use sub-workflows, and keep each step returning as little data as possible [1][2].
- **Store files externally and pass references?** The docs don’t directly recommend this pattern, but they do recommend reducing stored execution data and using filesystem/database modes for binary data instead of keeping it in memory [1][5].
- **Chunking/resumable processing:** the docs specifically mention splitting data into smaller chunks and using `Split In Batches` plus `Execute Workflow` for sub-workflows [2][4].

If you’re still hitting crashes or need a more specific design for your setup, please contact n8n support or ask in the n8n community forum.

   - Add a README and include your nodes/credentials in the package’s `n8n` section [1][8].
   - Publish to npm using **GitHub Actions with a provenance statement** [1][4][8].
   - Submit it for verification through the **n8n Creator Portal** [1][4].

3. **Important Cloud limitation**
   - On Cloud, you can only install the nodes n8n has already vetted and exposed in the editor [3][6].
   - If your goal is just to use Neo4j right now, you’d need a node that is already in that verified set, or run n8n self-hosted and install the npm package there [6].

You’re trying to prevent duplicate side effects after a partial failure, and the safest production pattern is to make each external step idempotent and store progress outside the workflow.

1. **Use idempotency keys for every API call that can create/update something**
   - This is general API design, not n8n-specific.
   - Send the same `orderId`-based key on retries, so the external service can treat repeats as the same request.

2. **Persist step state in your own database/table**
   - Store one row per order, e.g. `orderId`, `payment_status`, `inventory_status`, `shipping_status`, `last_completed_step`.
   - Update the row **after** each successful API call.
   - On retry, read the row first and branch around completed steps.

3. **Split the workflow into smaller pieces if you want cleaner recovery**
   - Use a parent workflow to orchestrate and a sub-workflow per stage.
   - n8n packages treat sub-workflows as dependencies when exporting/importing [6], but this doesn’t itself provide resume logic.

4. **Do not rely on partial executions for production recovery**
   - Partial executions are mainly for testing and debugging [4].
   - They’re not a durable checkpoint/replay mechanism.

5. **If you want a status-based error model, capture the failure cause**
   - In custom nodes, n8n supports `failure` declarations like `rate-limited`, `temporarily-unavailable`, `credential-invalid`, etc. [2]
   - That helps classify errors, but it still doesn’t resume workflow state by itself.

If you want, I can sketch a concrete pattern for n8n using:
- a **state table**,
- an **IF/Switch branch** for each step,
- and a **resume-from-last-success** flow.

It misses the key step of checking the API's status before retrying, which covers a crash after the call but before the checkpoint was saved. Points 3 to 5 are tangential filler (package export, custom-node failure declarations) that don't help the customer, though they are not harmful.

The reply directly and accurately addresses the architectural design question by recommending idempotency keys combined with external state tracking (such as a database table) to branch around already-completed steps upon retry. While it pulls in a couple of tangential points from the provided retrieval passages (such as node error declarations and package exports), these do not mislead the customer.

Reply gives the reference's core production pattern: stable orderId-based idempotency keys plus external DB state table with branching to skip completed steps, so retry resumes instead of duplicating. It correctly warns partial executions are not production recovery and sub-workflows alone do not provide resume. Missing explicit API status GET check is mitigated by idempotent retry with same key, so no material error.

The likely answer is: **“Both” sends both HTML and plain-text parts in one email, and the recipient’s email client chooses which part to display** [1].

1. In **Send Email → Email Format**, choose:
   - **HTML** if you want the message to be primarily HTML, or
   - **Both** if you want a plain-text fallback too [1].

2. With **Both**, n8n does **not** pick one version for the recipient; it includes both parts in the message, and the mail client decides which to render. That’s standard email behavior, not something n8n controls.

3. For your QR/logo case:
   - Keep the **QR code as a real attachment** as you’re already doing.
   - Also include the QR in the **HTML body** if you want it visible inline.
   - Use a meaningful plain-text fallback in case a client shows text only.

4. There is always some risk that a client shows the text part instead of HTML. Most modern clients like Gmail, iCloud Mail, Yandex, and Mail.ru usually render HTML, but I can’t guarantee every recipient’s settings or security filters won’t force text-only. That’s general email-client behavior.

5. Best practice for paying customers:
   - Put the **critical QR code in the attachment** as the source of truth.
   - Keep the HTML version as a convenience display.
   - Make the plain-text body clearly point users to the attachment.
   - Avoid depending on inline images alone for anything essential.

If you want, I can help you draft a robust HTML/plain-text email structure for this ticket flow.

You’re seeing expected session-based behavior: n8n chat memory keeps history for the current session, not a cross-thread “semantic memory” that can infer a location from a brand-new conversation. [2][6]

1. If you want the agent to remember across turns, make sure both turns use the same **Session Key** in the **MongoDB Chat Memory** node. That key is what ties messages to one memory thread. [5]
2. If you start a **new chat thread**, that is a **new session**, so the agent will not automatically reuse the previous thread’s context. n8n notes that “memory doesn’t persist between sessions.” [6]
3. If you have more than one memory node in the workflow, n8n says they share the same memory instance by default unless you set **different session IDs**. [1][3][4][7][8]
4. The **Context Window Length** only controls how many prior interactions from that session are considered; it does not turn memory into long-term retrieval or semantic search. [5]

So your interpretation is mostly correct: this is closest to **working/session memory**, not semantic, episodic, or procedural memory as those are usually described in AI theory.

For documentation, the clearest n8n references are:
- **What’s memory in AI?** [2]
- **MongoDB Chat Memory node** [5]
- **Conversational AI Agent** memory note [6]

If you want “pull out three facts from this location” to work in a new thread, you’ll need to either:
- pass the location explicitly in the new message, or
- build a separate lookup step against MongoDB based on your own search logic, rather than relying on chat memory alone. That last part is general workflow/DB design, not an n8n-specific memory feature.

If you want, I can help you map this workflow into either:
- true session memory, or
- a retrieval flow that searches MongoDB by location name before the agent პასუხs.

A good pattern here is to use an **Error Workflow** for recovery, and design your main workflow so repeated runs are safe and don’t duplicate side effects.

1. **Turn on execution saving where it helps recovery**
   - In **Workflow Settings**, enable **Save failed production executions** and, if needed, **Save execution progress** [5].
   - `Save execution progress` can let n8n resume from where it stopped after an error, but it may add latency [5].

2. **Create a separate error workflow**
   - Add an **Error Trigger** as the first node in a new workflow [6].
   - In the main workflow, go to **Options > Settings** and set **Error workflow** to that handler [6].
   - In the error workflow, save the failure context, notify someone, or create a recovery task.

3. **Make retries idempotent**
   - Since n8n does not give you a general “checkpoint and resume any node” feature in the docs, the safer approach is to persist progress in your own system.
   - For example, after **Validate** and **Process Data**, write a record like:
     - workflow/run ID
     - external API request ID
     - status = `processed`, `sent`, `saved`
   - On retry, check that record first and skip steps already completed. This is general workflow design, not n8n-specific.

4. **Stop automatic retries when the step is no longer transient**
   - Retry only for temporary failures like rate limits or network errors.
   - If the workflow keeps failing at the same business-rule step, route to manual review from the error workflow.
   - If the failure is due to memory pressure, note that n8n may stop executions with memory-related errors [1], and you may need to reduce payload size or redesign processing.

5. **If you’re dealing with large partial executions in the editor**
   - n8n can hit limits with partial executions on large workflows; the docs suggest using a **Limit** node temporarily while testing [3].

If you want, I can help you sketch an idempotent n8n pattern for your exact node chain (`Webhook → Validate → Process Data → External API → Save Result`).

The node is almost certainly being blocked by n8n’s file-access restriction, and the env vars you set are not the ones n8n documents for this node.  

1. On self-hosted n8n, control this with `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` [1]. In n8n 2.x, if you don’t set it explicitly, the default is `~/.n8n-files` [1], so `/home/node/.n8n/references/test.ico` would be outside the allowed area.

2. Set the allowed path explicitly to the directory you want to write to. For your Docker setup, that means something like:
```bash
-e N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/home/node/.n8n/references
```
You can include multiple allowed paths as a semicolon-separated list [1].

3. Make sure the target path is inside that allowed directory and use an absolute path, which n8n recommends [1]. For example:
- `File Path and Name`: `/home/node/.n8n/references/test.ico`

4. Keep the directory mounted into the container. You already have `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n`, so that part is fine. If you want `/data`, you’d need to mount it and also add it to `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` [1].

5. If you still get the error after that, check whether your instance has additional node blocking in place via `NODES_EXCLUDE` [3]. That setting can disable the Read/Write Files from Disk node entirely, but it would usually stop the node from being available rather than just blocking a path.

Important: the docs excerpt you shared does not mention `N8N_ALLOW_WRITE_TO_DISK` or `N8N_ALLOW_LIST_PATH`, so I can’t confirm those are valid for this node [1][2]. 

If you want, I can help you rewrite your exact `docker run` command with the correct variable placement.

295919.text:
You’re seeing a classic webhook retry/idempotency problem: n8n will run each incoming webhook execution, so duplicate deliveries can produce duplicate side effects.

What matters most is **how your external service retries** and **whether you’re in self-hosted queue mode or regular mode**, because that changes which n8n controls can help. n8n’s queue mode and concurrency controls do **not** provide event-id deduplication by themselves [1][4][7].

If you want the clean production pattern, it’s usually:

1. **Use your `event_id` as an idempotency key in your database**
   - Create a unique constraint on `event_id`.
   - On first receipt, insert a “seen” row before doing side effects.
   - If the insert fails because the row already exists, exit early.
   - This is general database/idempotency practice, not an n8n-specific feature.

2. **Keep the webhook workflow very short**
   - Webhook → validate → “dedupe/claim” step → return response immediately.
   - Then continue processing only if the claim succeeds.
   - In n8n terms, this is commonly done with a **Webhook** trigger [5] plus a DB/HTTP step after it.

3. **If you are self-hosted and using queue mode, enable concurrency controls only as a throughput safeguard**
   - `N8N_CONCURRENCY_PRODUCTION_LIMIT` can reduce how many production executions run at once [7].
   - This helps with overload, but it does **not** stop the same `event_id` from being processed twice.

4. **Do not rely on Redis locks alone unless you fully own the failure modes**
   - They can help, but your source of truth should still be the DB unique key.

If you want, send:
- whether you’re **self-hosted or n8n Cloud**
- whether you’re in **queue mode**
- your DB type

and I can suggest the safest n8n workflow pattern for your setup.

grades.why: The core fix matches the accepted answer: unique constraint on event_id, insert before side effects, skip if it already exists. It also covers responding quickly. Minor imprecision (concurrency limit framed as queue-mode-only, no concrete SQL or n8n node such as Skip on Conflict or Remove Duplicates) doesn't change what the customer does; the closing request for details is mild filler.

The reply correctly provides the standard idempotency pattern recommended in the reference packet: inserting the event ID into a database with a unique constraint before executing side effects, and acknowledging the webhook quickly to reduce retry triggers.

5. If you already have many nodes using that credential, updating the credential in place is the safest path; if you create a brand-new credential, you’ll need to reselect it on each node that uses Salesforce.

For prioritization: Salesforce’s docs note Connected Apps are being deprecated in favor of External Client Apps, but n8n’s docs also say existing Connected Apps continue to work [2]. 255850.text:
You’re rebuilding the ticket list on every loop pass, instead of loading it once and reusing it.

1. **Fetch the 1000+ Linear tickets once, outside the loop.**
   - Put the ticket fetch on its own branch before the loop.
   - The Loop Over Items node keeps its original incoming data and outputs batches through its **loop** output, then combines results on **done** [2].

2. **Do the PR loop separately.**
   - Feed the PRs into **Loop Over Items**.
   - Set **Batch Size** to whatever you need [3].

3. **Join the preloaded tickets without re-running that fetch.**
   - Don’t place the ticket-fetch node inside the loop.
   - If you need the ticket list available in every iteration, use a node that preserves data from earlier items, or a **Code** node with item linking if you are creating new items [6].

4. **If you use a Merge node, remember it waits for both inputs.**
   - Merge combines streams only when both inputs are available [4][7].
   - That means it’s not a “static lookup table” by itself inside a loop.
   - If both branches are inside the loop, both branches will execute every iteration.

5. **Best pattern for your case:**
   - Load tickets once.
   - Load PRs.
   - In the loop, extract the Linear ticket number from the PR.
   - Use a lookup/filter step against the already-loaded ticket data.
   - If you need to create new items in **Code**, set `pairedItem` so later nodes can still reference the original PR item [6].

If you want, I can sketch the exact node layout for:
- **Load tickets once → loop PRs → enrich by ticket number**, or
- a **Code node** approach that does the lookup in memory.

It never gives the reference's key step: drop the loop and use a Merge node that matches on the ticket ID (for example Enrich Input 1) or an Aggregate. It is vague ('a node that preserves data', 'lookup/filter step') and ends with an offer to sketch the layout, so the customer would likely have to come back.

The customer's core issue is an architectural misconception: they are attempting to loop and merge within a loop when n8n naturally handles item lists without explicit loops. The correct solution is to remove the loop entirely and merge the PR and Linear data using a Merge node set to Combine by Matching Fields. Instead, the reply reinforces the loop structure and recommends a vague, non-existent 'lookup/filter step' inside the loop.
grades.error: The reply tells the customer to keep the loop and use a lookup/filter step inside it against data fetched outside the loop, rather than removing the loop and combining the datasets directly with a Merge node by matching fields.

You’re running into a memory-limit / binary-data handling problem, and the docs already confirm the main fixes — but you’ve tried the usual ones and it still sounds like a design or execution-path issue that needs a human to review.

What the docs support:
- Large files can crash n8n when binary data stays in memory [1][8].
- For self-hosted n8n, set `N8N_DEFAULT_BINARY_DATA_MODE=filesystem` to move binary data off memory; if you’re using queue mode, use `database` instead, because `filesystem` is not supported there [1].
- For n8n Cloud, the recommended path is to reduce memory use by splitting data into smaller chunks, avoiding unnecessary saved execution data, and splitting heavy work into sub-workflows that return only small results [2][4][8].

What I’d check meanwhile:
- Whether your flow is running in queue mode and whether binary mode matches it (`database` for queue mode) [1].
- Whether the Webhook response or final upload step is returning a very large payload; large webhook responses have separate limits and offloading behavior in queue mode [6].
- Whether you’re saving full successful executions, which can add pressure in Cloud [4].

This now needs a human review because the docs don’t cover resumable processing/retry design in enough detail, and you’ve already tried the standard mitigations. For a likely workflow/runtime issue, please post this to the n8n community forum or open a GitHub issue on `n8n-io/n8n` if you suspect a bug.

You’re looking for the verified-community-node process: on n8n Cloud, only a select set of **verified** community nodes can be installed in the editor, so a Neo4j package may simply not be in that curated set yet [3].

1. **Check whether the node is verified and Cloud-available**
   - In Cloud, installable community nodes come from the **Nodes panel** only when they’re in n8n’s verified list [3].
   - Unverified npm community nodes are **not available on n8n Cloud** [6].

2. **If you want to submit a node**
   - Build it as an npm package using the `n8n-node` scaffolding/tool [1][8].
   - Make sure it follows the verified-node guidelines, including **no runtime dependencies** [1][4][8].
   - Add a README and include your nodes/credentials in the package’s `n8n` section [1][8].
   - Publish to npm using **GitHub Actions with a provenance statement** [1][4][8].
   - Submit it for verification through the **n8n Creator Portal** [1][4].

3. **Important Cloud limitation**
   - On Cloud, you can only install the nodes n8n has already vetted and exposed in the editor [3][6].
   - If your goal is just to use Neo4j right now, you’d need a node that is already in that verified set, or run n8n self-hosted and install the npm package there [6].

The approval flow is documented across the “Submit community nodes” and “building community nodes” docs [1][4][8]. If you want, I can also outline the exact submission checklist for a new community node.

You’re running into a memory-limit / binary-data handling problem, and the docs already confirm the main fixes — but you’ve tried the usual ones and it still sounds like a design or execution-path issue that needs a human to review.

What the docs support:
- Large files can crash n8n when binary data stays in memory [1][8].
- For self-hosted n8n, set `N8N_DEFAULT_BINARY_DATA_MODE=filesystem` to move binary data off memory; if you’re using queue mode, use `database` instead, because `filesystem` is not supported there [1].
- For n8n Cloud, the recommended path is to reduce memory use by splitting data into smaller chunks, avoiding unnecessary saved execution data, and splitting heavy work into sub-workflows that return only small results [2][4][8].

What I’d check meanwhile:
- Whether your flow is running in queue mode and whether binary mode matches it (`database` for queue mode) [1].
- Whether the Webhook response or final upload step is returning a very large payload; large webhook responses have separate limits and offloading behavior in queue mode [6].
- Whether you’re saving full successful executions, which can add pressure in Cloud [4].

This now needs a human review because the docs don’t cover resumable processing/retry design in enough detail, and you’ve already tried the standard mitigations. For a likely workflow/runtime issue, please post this to the n8n community forum or open a GitHub issue on `n8n-io/n8n` if you suspect a bug.

Handoff summary:

You’re looking for the verified-community-node process: on n8n Cloud, only a select set of **verified** community nodes can be installed in the editor, so a Neo4j package may simply not be in that curated set yet [3].

1. **Check whether the node is verified and Cloud-available**
   - In Cloud, installable community nodes come from the **Nodes panel** only when they’re in n8n’s verified list [3].
   - Unverified npm community nodes are **not available on n8n Cloud** [6].

2. **If you want to submit a node**
   - Build it as an npm package using the `n8n-node` scaffolding/tool [1][8].
   - Make sure it follows the verified-node guidelines, including **no runtime dependencies** [1][4][8].
   - Add a README and include your nodes/credentials in the package’s `n8n` section [1][8].
   - Publish to npm using **GitHub Actions with a provenance statement** [1][4][8].
   - Submit it for verification through the **n8n Creator Portal** [1][4].

3. **Important Cloud limitation**
   - On Cloud, you can only install the nodes n8n has already vetted and exposed in the editor [3][6].
   - If your goal is just to use Neo4j right now, you’d need a node that is already in that verified set, or run n8n self-hosted and install the npm package there [6].

You’re trying to prevent duplicate side effects after a partial failure, and the safest production pattern is to make each external step idempotent and store progress outside the workflow.

1. **Use idempotency keys for every API call that can create/update something**
   - This is general API design, not n8n-specific.
   - Send the same `orderId`-based key on retries, so the external service can treat repeats as the same request.

2. **Persist step state in your own database/table**
   - Store one row per order, e.g. `orderId`, `payment_status`, `inventory_status`, `shipping_status`, `last_completed_step`.
   - Update the row **after** each successful API call.
   - On retry, read the row first and branch around completed steps.

3. **Split the workflow into smaller pieces if you want cleaner recovery**
   - Use a parent workflow to orchestrate and a sub-workflow per stage.
   - n8n packages treat sub-workflows as dependencies when exporting/importing [6], but this doesn’t itself provide resume logic.

4. **Do not rely on partial executions for production recovery**
   - Partial executions are mainly for testing and debugging [4].
   - They’re not a durable checkpoint/replay mechanism.

5. **If you want a status-based error model, capture the failure cause**
   - In custom nodes, n8n supports `failure` declarations like `rate-limited`, `temporarily-unavailable`, `credential-invalid`, etc. [2]
   - That helps classify errors, but it still doesn’t resume workflow state by itself.

If you want, I can sketch a concrete pattern for n8n using:
- a **state table**,
- an **IF/Switch branch** for each step,
- and a **resume-from-last-success** flow.

It misses the key step of checking the API's status before retrying, which covers a crash after the call but before the checkpoint was saved. Points 3 to 5 are tangential filler (package export, custom-node failure declarations) that don't help the customer, though they are not harmful.

The reply directly and accurately addresses the architectural design question by recommending idempotency keys combined with external state tracking (such as a database table) to branch around already-completed steps upon retry. While it pulls in a couple of tangential points from the provided retrieval passages (such as node error declarations and package exports), these do not mislead the customer.

Reply gives the reference's core production pattern: stable orderId-based idempotency keys plus external DB state table with branching to skip completed steps, so retry resumes instead of duplicating. 297787.text:
The likely answer is: **“Both” sends both HTML and plain-text parts in one email, and the recipient’s email client chooses which part to display** [1].

1. In **Send Email → Email Format**, choose:
   - **HTML** if you want the message to be primarily HTML, or
   - **Both** if you want a plain-text fallback too [1].

2. With **Both**, n8n does **not** pick one version for the recipient; it includes both parts in the message, and the mail client decides which to render. That’s standard email behavior, not something n8n controls.

3. For your QR/logo case:
   - Keep the **QR code as a real attachment** as you’re already doing.
   - Also include the QR in the **HTML body** if you want it visible inline.
   - Use a meaningful plain-text fallback in case a client shows text only.

4. There is always some risk that a client shows the text part instead of HTML. Most modern clients like Gmail, iCloud Mail, Yandex, and Mail.ru usually render HTML, but I can’t guarantee every recipient’s settings or security filters won’t force text-only. That’s general email-client behavior.

5. Best practice for paying customers:
   - Put the **critical QR code in the attachment** as the source of truth.
   - Keep the HTML version as a convenience display.
   - Make the plain-text body clearly point users to the attachment.
   - Avoid depending on inline images alone for anything essential.

If you want, I can help you draft a robust HTML/plain-text email structure for this ticket flow.

grades.why: The reply correctly explains that Both sends both parts in one message and the client decides. It says modern providers usually render HTML, with residual risk from user settings or filters, and advises keeping the QR as an attachment with a useful text fallback. This matches the reference. It omits alt text and the CID/Outlook caveat, and its step 1 about choosing HTML or Both is slightly tangential, but none of this is harmful.

The reply directly answers all of the user's questions accurately according to n8n documentation and standard email client behavior. It correctly explains that selecting 'Both' sends a multipart message containing both versions and leaves the rendering decision to the recipient's client, while offering sound best practices.

309298.text:
You’re seeing expected session-based behavior: n8n chat memory keeps history for the current session, not a cross-thread “semantic memory” that can infer a location from a brand-new conversation. [2][6]

1. If you want the agent to remember across turns, make sure both turns use the same **Session Key** in the **MongoDB Chat Memory** node. That key is what ties messages to one memory thread. [5]
2. If you start a **new chat thread**, that is a **new session**, so the agent will not automatically reuse the previous thread’s context. n8n notes that “memory doesn’t persist between sessions.” [6]
3. If you have more than one memory node in the workflow, n8n says they share the same memory instance by default unless you set **different session IDs**. [1][3][4][7][8]
4. The **Context Window Length** only controls how many prior interactions from that session are considered; it does not turn memory into long-term retrieval or semantic search. [5]

So your interpretation is mostly correct: this is closest to **working/session memory**, not semantic, episodic, or procedural memory as those are usually described in AI theory.

For documentation, the clearest n8n references are:
- **What’s memory in AI?** [2]
- **MongoDB Chat Memory node** [5]
- **Conversational AI Agent** memory note [6]

If you want “pull out three facts from this location” to work in a new thread, you’ll need to either:
- pass the location explicitly in the new message, or
- build a separate lookup step against MongoDB based on your own search logic, rather than relying on chat memory alone. That last part is general workflow/DB design, not an n8n-specific memory feature.

If you want, I can help you map this workflow into either:
- true session memory, or
- a retrieval flow that searches MongoDB by location name before the agent პასუხs.

grades.why: The reply correctly confirms the session-scoped working-memory interpretation and points to the right doc. Its fix for the cross-thread case is only generic (pass the location explicitly, or build a separate lookup). It misses the reference's key step of pre-loading from Mongo and injecting via Chat Memory Manager, and it doesn't explain that a tool is pull-based. It also ends with a garbled word ("პასუხs") and an offer of further help, which is filler. Because the right direction is given without the key mechanism, the fix is partial.

The reply accurately confirms that n8n chat memory is tied to session keys (working memory) and does not persist across new chat threads by default. It provides the relevant documentation links and explains how to approach cross-thread retrieval or persistent session management.

306976.text:
A good pattern here is to use an **Error Workflow** for recovery, and design your main workflow so repeated runs are safe and don’t duplicate side effects.

1. **Turn on execution saving where it helps recovery**
   - In **Workflow Settings**, enable **Save failed production executions** and, if needed, **Save execution progress** [5].
   - `Save execution progress` can let n8n resume from where it stopped after an error, but it may add latency [5].

2. **Create a separate error workflow**
   - Add an **Error Trigger** as the first node in a new workflow [6].
   - In the main workflow, go to **Options > Settings** and set **Error workflow** to that handler [6].
   - In the error workflow, save the failure context, notify someone, or create a recovery task.

3. **Make retries idempotent**
   - Since n8n does not give you a general “checkpoint and resume any node” feature in the docs, the safer approach is to persist progress in your own system.
   - For example, after **Validate** and **Process Data**, write a record like:
     - workflow/run ID
     - external API request ID
     - status = `processed`, `sent`, `saved`
   - On retry, check that record first and skip steps already completed. This is general workflow design, not n8n-specific.

4. **Stop automatic retries when the step is no longer transient**
   - Retry only for temporary failures like rate limits or network errors.
   - If the workflow keeps failing at the same business-rule step, route to manual review from the error workflow.
   - If the failure is due to memory pressure, note that n8n may stop executions with memory-related errors [1], and you may need to reduce payload size or redesign processing.

5. **If you’re dealing with large partial executions in the editor**
   - n8n can hit limits with partial executions on large workflows; the docs suggest using a **Limit** node temporarily while testing [3].

If you want, I can help you sketch an idempotent n8n pattern for your exact node chain (`Webhook → Validate → Process Data → External API → Save Result`).

grades.why: The reply matches the reference's core advice: save progress in your own store, make retries idempotent by checking a status record, retry only transient failures, and route repeated failures to manual review through an error workflow. It also adds n8n-specific settings that are real. Point 5 about partial executions in the editor is tangential padding, and the closing offer is mild filler; neither would cost the customer anything. It does not mention backoff explicitly or give a retry-count example, which is a minor gap.

The reply directly answers all of the customer's questions regarding recovering partially completed workflows, checkpoints, idempotency, and retry strategies. Migrating from Zapier to n8n usually means recreating the automation logic in n8n rather than doing a direct one-click import.

I can confirm two things from the docs:
1. n8n supports moving workflows between n8n accounts/instances by export/import JSON [2], and now also by n8n packages between n8n instances [1].
2. That does **not** cover Zapier-to-n8n migration directly, so there’s no built-in path documented here for importing Zapier zaps as-is.

The practical answer is: **you usually do have to rebuild the workflows**, but not necessarily from scratch in the sense of rethinking everything:
1. List each Zap’s trigger, steps, filters, and branching.
2. Recreate the trigger in n8n with the matching trigger node.
3. Rebuild each action step with the closest n8n node.
4. Recreate filters/paths with n8n logic nodes.
5. Test each workflow with sample data before turning it on.

If you want, I can help you estimate the effort if you paste one or two Zapier zaps here — I’ll tell you which parts map cleanly to n8n and which parts usually need redesign.

308724.text:
The node is almost certainly being blocked by n8n’s file-access restriction, and the env vars you set are not the ones n8n documents for this node.  

1. On self-hosted n8n, control this with `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` [1]. In n8n 2.x, if you don’t set it explicitly, the default is `~/.n8n-files` [1], so `/home/node/.n8n/references/test.ico` would be outside the allowed area.

2. Set the allowed path explicitly to the directory you want to write to. For your Docker setup, that means something like:
```bash
-e N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/home/node/.n8n/references
```
You can include multiple allowed paths as a semicolon-separated list [1].

3. Make sure the target path is inside that allowed directory and use an absolute path, which n8n recommends [1]. For example:
- `File Path and Name`: `/home/node/.n8n/references/test.ico`

4. Keep the directory mounted into the container. You already have `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n`, so that part is fine. If you want `/data`, you’d need to mount it and also add it to `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` [1].

5. If you still get the error after that, check whether your instance has additional node blocking in place via `NODES_EXCLUDE` [3]. That setting can disable the Read/Write Files from Disk node entirely, but it would usually stop the node from being available rather than just blocking a path.

Important: the docs excerpt you shared does not mention `N8N_ALLOW_WRITE_TO_DISK` or `N8N_ALLOW_LIST_PATH`, so I can’t confirm those are valid for this node [1][2]. 

If you want, I can help you rewrite your exact `docker run` command with the correct variable placement.

But its main example allow-lists a path inside /home/node/.n8n, which n8n always blocks, so the customer would hit the same error. The correct /data route appears only as a side note, with no chown of the host folder, and it hedges on the invalid variables rather than saying they do nothing.

The customer would repeat the same error. The reply also omits the host folder chown for /root/n8n_storage.

However, it specifically recommends setting this to a subfolder inside /home/node/.n8n, which is blocked by n8n's internal state protection rules and will cause the execution to fail again.

You’re running into a memory-limit / binary-data handling problem, and the docs already confirm the main fixes — but you’ve tried the usual ones and it still sounds like a design or execution-path issue that needs a human to review.

What the docs support:
- Large files can crash n8n when binary data stays in memory [1][8].

- Whether your flow is running in queue mode and whether binary mode matches it (`database` for queue mode) [1].
- Whether the Webhook response or final upload step is returning a very large payload; large webhook responses have separate limits and offloading behavior in queue mode [6].
- Whether you’re saving full successful executions, which can add pressure in Cloud [4].

This now needs a human review because the docs don’t cover resumable processing/retry design in enough detail, and you’ve already tried the standard mitigations. For a likely workflow/runtime issue, please post this to the n8n community forum or open a GitHub issue on `n8n-io/n8n` if you suspect a bug.

Yes—there is a submission and verification process; publishing a community node to npm alone doesn’t make it available on n8n Cloud. Cloud only supports verified community nodes. [6]

For an extension author, the process is:

1. **Build and test the node.** n8n recommends the `n8n-node` CLI. The package name must start with `n8n-nodes-` or `@<scope>/n8n-nodes-`, include the keyword `n8n-community-node-package`, and declare its nodes and credentials in the `package.json` `n8n` attribute. [8]
2. **Meet the verification requirements.** Follow the technical and UX guidelines, pass automated checks, and provide a README. Verified nodes must not use runtime dependencies. [1]
3. **Publish to npm and submit through the [n8n Creator Portal](https://creators.n8n.io/nodes).** From May 1, 2026, verification submissions must be published using GitHub Actions with a provenance statement. n8n fetches the package from npm for final vetting. [1]
4. **After verification, users can discover and install it from the Nodes panel**, including on Cloud. [1][3]

The full flow is documented in [Submit community nodes](https://docs.n8n.io/connect/create-nodes/deploy-your-node/submit-community-nodes).

I can’t confirm the particular Neo4j extension’s verification status without its package name or link. If it’s unverified, it requires self-hosted n8n rather than Cloud; its author would need to submit it for verification. [6]

Your first request works, so the key thing to check is whether pagination builds the correct URL—not to assume the credentials need more scopes.

**What is the exact value of `_links.next` in the successful response with pagination disabled?** You can redact your site identifier, but please preserve the URL’s path and query string.

Your **Next URL** expression currently concatenates:

```text
https://api.atlassian.com/ex/confluence/xyz
```

with that value. Whether this is correct depends on whether `_links.next` is an absolute URL, a relative path, or a query-only reference. The HTTP Request pagination docs explicitly require inspecting the response, because the **Next URL** expression depends on its structure. [1][4]

**If `_links.next` is already a complete `https://api.atlassian.com/...` URL**, set **Pagination Mode** to **Response Contains Next URL** and **Next URL** to:

```javascript
{{ $response.body._links.next }}
```

That follows the URL directly instead of adding another prefix. [4]

If it’s relative, please share its exact value before changing the expression. As a general HTTP point, an incorrectly constructed URL can reach a different endpoint and receive an authorization error; the `401` alone doesn’t establish that your working request lacks scopes.

Its conditional fix, `{{ $response.body._links.next }}`, would not fix it either, and it points the customer away from the real cause.

310338.text:
A whole-workflow retry can repeat successful API actions unless each step checks durable progress and prevents duplicates.

**I’d use a database state table plus per-step idempotency keys.** This is a general database/HTTP reliability pattern, not a claim about n8n’s built-in resume behavior.

1. **Persist checkpoints outside the execution.** Your returned object describes progress, but returning it doesn’t itself save a checkpoint. Use a table such as:
   ```text
   order_steps(
     order_id, step, status, idempotency_key,
     external_id, attempts, last_error
   )
   ```
   Add a unique constraint on `(order_id, step)`. Use statuses such as `pending`, `in_progress`, `completed`, and `needs_reconciliation`.

2. **Guard every API action.** Before `payment`, `inventory`, or `shipping`, read its record. Skip `completed` steps. Claim unfinished work atomically so concurrent retries cannot both start it.

3. **Reuse a stable idempotency key.** For example, `order:123:shipping:v1`. Send it using the API’s documented idempotency mechanism—not a fresh key on each attempt. Store the successful response’s external ID, then mark the step `completed`.

4. **Handle ambiguous failures separately.** A timeout can mean “shipping succeeded, but the response was lost.” Reuse the same key or query the provider before retrying. Without provider-side idempotency or reliable reconciliation, checkpoints alone cannot guarantee no duplicates.

5. **Retry transient failures with bounded backoff.** Route permanent failures for intervention; define compensating actions, such as refunds, where appropriate.

Sub-workflows can organize the implementation; they aren’t a replacement for durable checkpoints and deduplication. “Resume” here means re-entering the process and safely skipping completed steps.

grades.why: The reply recommends durable checkpoints plus stable idempotency keys. It also covers the key step from the reference: after an ambiguous failure, query the provider before retrying and reuse the same key. It adds sensible detail on the state table and atomic claiming, and it makes no false claims or unsafe suggestions. It does not name the status-check GET as explicitly as the reference, but it states the idea clearly.

The reply directly and accurately answers the customer's design pattern question. It correctly recommends using an external database state table for checkpoints combined with stable idempotency keys and API status checks/reconciliation to prevent duplicate actions.

The likely issue is that HTML extraction needs a selector and output field—it isn’t simply loading the downloaded HTML into a string.

1. In your **Google Drive** node, named **Download file**, confirm:
   - **Resource**: `File`
   - **Operation**: `Download`
   - **Put Output File in Field**: `data`
   - **Google File Conversion → Google Docs**: `HTML`

   These are the documented download/export settings; your shared JSON doesn’t explicitly show the HTML conversion selection. [1]

2. Replace **Extract from File** with an **HTML** node configured as:
   - **Operation**: `Extract HTML Content`
   - **Source Data**: `Binary`
   - **Input Binary Field**: `data`
   - Under **Extraction Values**:
     - **Key**: `content`
     - **CSS Selector**: `body`
     - **Return Value**: `HTML`
     - **Return Array**: off. [3]

This extracts the HTML *inside* the document’s `<body>` into the `content` field—not the complete original HTML file, including its `<head>`. The selector `body` is standard HTML/CSS usage.

If you want readable text instead of markup, use **Return Value → Text** with the same selector. [3]

With **Both**, n8n sends both formats; the recipient’s email client—not n8n or your SMTP provider—chooses which to display. [1] Your attached QR is a useful fallback.

1. **Both means both formats in one email, not two emails or a sender-side choice.** n8n documents that both formats are sent and the recipient’s client selects the display format. [1] In standard email terminology, this is a MIME alternative: plain text and HTML represent the same message.

2. **HTML is normal, but not guaranteed.** Gmail, Yandex, Mail.ru, and iCloud generally support HTML email. However, the app used to read the mailbox, user preferences, and security settings can result in plain-text display or blocked images. These are general email-client behaviors, not n8n-specific. Importantly, **displaying HTML doesn’t guarantee displaying its images**.

3. **Keep the ticket usable without inline images.**
   - Keep **Send Email → Email Format → Both** for a readable fallback. [1]
   - Keep the QR file attached. In **Options → Attachments**, specify the binary property containing the QR; multiple properties use a comma-separated list. [1]
   - Make the text version explicitly say: “Your QR ticket is attached.”
   - If possible, include a secure ticket-download link and a human-readable ticket reference in both versions.

4. **Test delivered messages**, not just the HTML preview: check those providers in webmail and mobile apps, with images blocked and plain-text viewing enabled where available.

There’s no way to guarantee HTML/inline QR rendering for every paying customer; attachment and text fallbacks are the reliable approach.

The likely cause is interference between simultaneous writes using the default append method—not necessarily failed webhook delivery.

Your JSON doesn’t set **Use Append**. The documented default adds empty rows or columns before writing data, rather than using Google’s append endpoint. That makes **Use Append** the first change to test, although the excerpts don’t confirm your specific race condition. [1]

1. Open your Google Sheets node, **Append row in sheet**, and keep **Operation → Append Row**. Keep the existing `Link photo` mapping:
   ```javascript
   {{ $json.body.secure_url }}
   ```
   Manual column mapping is supported for this operation. [7]

2. Under **Options**, add **Use Append** and turn it **on**. This switches to Google’s `spreadsheets.values.append` endpoint and reduces the separate API calls involved in adding rows. [1]

3. Check that the sheet’s data is contiguous, without blank-row gaps or breaks between columns. The documentation warns that **Use Append** can place data incorrectly when those gaps exist. [1]

4. Repeat a small bulk upload using distinct URLs. Compare the URLs received in successful executions against the resulting sheet rows. This is a general diagnostic check: it distinguishes missing writes from repeated payloads or data landing elsewhere.

This is a documented alternative write path, **not a guaranteed concurrency fix**. Also, adding the same delay to every execution would not serialize simultaneous requests; they could still reach the write step together.
</reply>

Toggling 'Use Append' still sends concurrent calls to the Google Sheets API, which is non-atomic and will continue to lose rows under simultaneous webhook triggers. 306976.text:
Your main risk is repeating successful external actions when retrying a partially completed workflow.

Use n8n’s saved progress alongside durable checkpoints—not retries alone.

1. **Save execution progress.** In workflow settings, set **Save execution progress** to **Save**. The docs describe this as allowing the workflow to resume where it stopped after an error, with possible added latency. Also enable **Save failed production executions** for investigation. [5] This isn’t a documented guarantee of automatic retries or recovery from every crash.

2. **Add a separate error workflow.** Create a workflow beginning with **Error Trigger**, save it, then select it under the production workflow’s **Options → Settings → Error workflow**. Use it to alert or initiate your recovery process. [6] Don’t assume it automatically contains a complete recovery checkpoint.

3. **Persist business checkpoints.** This is general reliability design: assign each request a stable job ID and store its payload reference, completed stages, API result/reference, attempt count, and last error in durable storage. Recovery should read that record and skip completed stages. For large payloads, store references rather than duplicating the data.

4. **Make external writes idempotent and bound retries.** Where supported, reuse the same API idempotency key for every attempt. A timeout can mean “accepted, but response lost”; reconcile the API’s state before repeating the action. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, respecting `Retry-After`. As a starting policy, stop after five attempts or 15 minutes. Send permanent validation/authentication failures—and ambiguous outcomes you cannot reconcile—to manual review.

The key distinction: **saved execution progress supports resumption; durable checkpoints and idempotency prevent duplicated business effects.**

It adds the n8n-specific settings (Save execution progress, Error Trigger error workflow) and states their limits honestly. The five-attempts-or-15-minutes cutoff is offered only as a starting policy, so it is not an error.

The reply directly answers the architectural questions about designing resilient and recoverable workflows. It correctly recommends combining checkpoints, idempotency, bounded retries with backoff, error workflows, and moving failed executions to manual review, aligning closely with the reference solution.

The likely cause of the unreliable answers is leaving retrieval to the model’s discretion; stricter prompts won’t make that deterministic, and the execution failure needs separate diagnosis.

For your Instagram/Facebook bot, prioritize **retrieval-first orchestration**, not a larger system prompt:

1. **Retrieve before generating.** As a general LLM architecture pattern, run your Supabase search as a required application step—not an optional tool the agent decides whether to call. Pass the returned records to the model for wording only. For images, first extract search attributes, then follow the same retrieval path.

2. **Enforce a no-results branch.** If retrieval returns nothing or fails, send a predefined clarification or unavailable-response message. Don’t ask the model to fill the gap.

3. **Validate before sending.** Require product IDs in generated output and verify them against retrieved records. Populate prices, stock, and links directly from Supabase. Reject unsupported products. This is general application-level validation, not prompt enforcement.

4. **Inspect agent overhead.** On the **AI Agent (Tools Agent)**, turn **Return Intermediate Steps** on and inspect calls. **Max Iterations** defaults to `10`; lowering it limits model iterations, **not elapsed execution time or input length**. [2]

5. **Bound conversation input.** Keep recent turns plus a compact summary; limit retrieved records and per-record text. Treat history as conversational context, never authoritative product data. These are general LLM practices.

The likely cause is n8n 2.x’s default file-access restriction, not the directory ownership you already changed.

1. **Allow your mounted storage directory explicitly.** Starting in n8n 2.0, `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` defaults to `~/.n8n-files`, which excludes all the paths you tried. Add this to your Docker run command: [1]
   ```bash
   -e N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/data \
   ```
   This is the documented control for file access—not the `N8N_ALLOW_WRITE_TO_DISK` or `N8N_ALLOW_LIST_PATH` variables you added. Multiple allowed directories can be separated with semicolons. [1]

2. **Recreate the container with the updated command.** Environment changes require creating a new container (general Docker behavior):
   ```bash
   docker stop n8n
   docker rm n8n
   ```
   Then rerun your original command with the environment change above, retaining both volume mounts. Removing the container this way does not delete your named volume or host storage directory.

3. **Use the mounted path in your node.** Keep **Read/Write Files from Disk → Write File to Disk**, and set:
   - **File Path and Name:** `/data/test.ico`
   - Keep **Input Binary Field:** `data`

   `/data` refers to the container directory mounted from `/root/n8n_storage`, not a host path. [1][2]

4. **Check filesystem permissions separately**, using general Linux checks:
   ```bash
   docker exec n8n sh -c 'id; ls -ld /data; test -w /data && echo writable'
   ```
   If it isn’t writable, grant the displayed process user write access to the host directory.

Use `/data` for your files rather than the internal-state directory `/home/node/.n8n`.

grades.why: The reply reaches the reference's key fix: set N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/data, recreate the container, and write to /data. It correctly says the two variables the customer added are not the real controls, and it steers them away from /home/node/.n8n. It covers host directory permissions only as a generic check rather than the specific chown of /root/n8n_storage, but the check is sound and the main fix is complete. It says nothing unsafe: removing the container keeps the volumes.

The reply correctly identifies that n8n 2.x restricts file operations to ~/.n8n-files by default and provides the correct environment variable (N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/data) to grant access to the mounted volume. It also explains how to update the Docker command and advises against using n8n's internal state directory.
